timelineEvents.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
timelineEvents.label: 1933 · Berlin–Vienna–Paris migration
timelineEvents.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Following Nazi persecution, Kaper and Jurmann flee Berlin after UFA terminates Jewish employees' contracts. Decisive moment: Kaper and his wife are attacked by Nazi gang on main Berlin street. Both composers relocate to Paris.

timelineEvents.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
timelineEvents.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper arrives in New York from France with Eleonora, holding a temporary visa and travelling onward to Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora arrived in New York aboard the S.S. Champlain from Le Havre on 24 October 1934, with Los Angeles listed as their destination.

timelineEvents.title: The Sängerfilm and the star-singer circuit
timelineEvents.label: Sängerfilm circuit
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann’s songs entered the Sängerfilm economy, where screen performance, star singers, sheet music, records, radio, and dance-band repertory reinforced one another.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The Kaper–Jurmann partnership developed inside the commercial ecology of early European musical film. Their songs for productions associated with singers such as Richard Tauber and Jan Kiepura were not simply film numbers: they were designed to travel beyond the screen as printed music, recordings, radio items, and repertory for performers. This star-singer circuit explains why the duo’s European experience later appeared useful to MGM, which read it through the promotional language of Viennese musical competence.

timelineEvents.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
timelineEvents.label: Transnational sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

timelineEvents.title: Ninon reaches Louis B. Mayer: the Ritz meeting and MGM contract
timelineEvents.label: Ninon opens the MGM path
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The European success of Ninon reportedly brought Kaper and Jurmann to the attention of Louis B. Mayer, leading to a meeting at the Hôtel Ritz and an MGM contract.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper later recalled that the success of Ninon—written for Tout pour l’amour, the French version of Ein Lied für Dich—was the turning point that opened the path to Hollywood. During his European talent-scouting trip in August 1934, Louis B. Mayer reportedly asked to meet the song’s authors, heard them perform at the Hôtel Ritz, and offered a seven-year MGM contract.

timelineEvents.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
timelineEvents.label: MGM’s “Viennese” label
timelineEvents.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers” and as a brilliant Viennese musical team. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity.

places.authorizedName: French Line Pier 57, North River, foot of West 15th Street, Manhattan, New York
places.publicNote: Approximate arrival site for Kaper and Eleonora's 1934 Atlantic crossing from Le Havre aboard the S.S. Champlain. In this period the French Line (Compagnie Générale Transatlantique) used Pier 57 on the North River, at the foot of West 15th Street; the pier is inferred from the line's documented berth rather than named in the passenger manifest. The record establishes arrival at New York but not processing at Ellis Island.

French port city context for Kaper's 1934 Atlantic crossing from Le Havre to New York aboard the S.S. Champlain. The marker is placed at city level: in 1934 CGT liners still used the port's earlier transatlantic quays, since the landmark Gare Maritime on the quai Johannès-Couvert opened only in May 1935 (with the Normandie) and was destroyed in the 1944 bombing of Le Havre.

Vienna functions here as a European music-film and publicity context for the Berlin–Paris–Hollywood route and the star-singer circuit. MGM’s later “Viennese composers” label is not presented as Kaper’s biographical origin.

Major German film-production centre associated with the multiple-language version system in early European sound cinema. The marker represents the broader historic Babelsberg studio complex; no individual stage or production building is asserted for the linked context.
French studio/production-centre context for early sound-film multiple-language version production.

West Berlin district context for Kaper's settled Berlin position before the 1933 forced departure. His address is identified as Pommersche Straße in Wilmersdorf, an affluent western Berlin residential district.

Documented Berlin residence: the Berliner Adreßbuch 1932 lists B. Kaper, composer, at Pommersche Straße 3 in Wilmersdorf. A later official planning record identifies the historical corner parcel as Sächsische Straße 48–49 / Pommersche Straße 3–4. Numbers 3–4 are absent from the present official address register, so the marker locates the historical corner parcel approximately rather than a surviving entrance.
